name: Rwandan Isombe
description: Isombe, Rwanda's everyday hero dish, is genuinely built from pounded cassava leaves cooked down with real eggplant, bell pepper, and peanut butter into a thick, velvety green stew - eggplant is a real, defining ingredient here, not an optional add-in, and real cassava leaves aren't a distinct item here, so spinach stands in for a milder, less fibrous approximation.

ingredients_full.note: standing in for pounded cassava leaves

ingredients.note: standing in for pounded cassava leaves

steps_detailed: Cook the onion in the palm oil 3-4 minutes.
Add the eggplant and bell pepper, and cook 5-6 minutes until slightly softened.
Add the spinach and a splash of water, cover, and simmer 20-25 minutes until everything is tender.
Stir in the peanut butter and simmer uncovered 10 minutes more until thickened.
steps: Cook the onion in the palm oil 3-4 minutes.

name: Rwandan Ugali
description: Ugali, a stiff maize porridge, is a Rwandan staple starch shared with much of East Africa, traditionally served alongside isombe and other stews.
steps_detailed: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.
Gradually beat in the remaining cornmeal, stirring constantly, over medium-low heat 12-15 minutes, until very thick and smooth.

name: Rwandan Ibihaza
description: Ibihaza, pumpkin stewed with beans until it breaks down into a thick, hearty dish, is a genuine Rwandan staple, real technique cooking the squash until it nearly falls apart, thickening the stew naturally.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

ingredients.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

steps_detailed: Cook the onion 3-4 minutes.
Add the squash and enough water to just cover, and simmer 25-28 minutes, mashing some of the squash as it softens, until it breaks down and thickens the stew.
Add the cowpeas and simmer 5-8 minutes more to warm through.

name: Rwandan Agatogo
description: Agatogo, plantain and cassava stewed together with meat, is a beloved Rwandan dish, real technique simmering the starches long enough to become genuinely tender before mashing lightly together.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef, 6-7 minutes.
Add the plantain, cassava, and tomatoes with enough water to cover, and simmer 30-35 minutes until the starches are completely tender.
Mash lightly together, leaving some texture.

name: Rwandan Brochettes
description: Brochettes, grilled meat skewers, are a beloved Rwandan street food and social staple, often centered around goat - beef stands in here as a more widely available substitute.
steps_detailed: Marinate the beef in the garlic and lemon juice 15-20 minutes.
Thread onto skewers and grill, turning, 10-12 minutes, until charred and cooked through.
steps: Marinate the beef in the garlic and lemon juice 15-20 minutes.

name: Rwandan Umutsima
description: Umutsima, a stiff cassava porridge, is a genuine Rwandan staple starch, closely related to ugali but made from cassava flour rather than maize - cassava flour isn't a distinct item here, so cornmeal stands in for a similarly stiff texture.
steps_detailed: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.
Gradually beat in the remaining cornmeal, stirring constantly, over medium-low heat 15-18 minutes, until very thick.
steps: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.

name: Rwandan Sombe
description: A variation of isombe made with real coconut milk added for richness, common in some Rwandan households.
steps_detailed: Cook the garlic in a little oil 1 minute.
Add the spinach and simmer 12-15 minutes.
Stir in the coconut milk and peanut butter, and simmer 8-10 minutes more until thickened.

name: Rwandan Fried Plantain
description: Fried ripe plantain, a common Rwandan side dish, real versions using genuinely ripe plantain for real caramelization.
steps_detailed: Fry the plantain slices in the oil, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized and golden.
steps: Fry the plantain slices in the oil, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized and golden.

description: Sweetened milk tea (icyayi) is a beloved daily ritual across Rwanda, reflecting genuine East African tea culture.

Stir in the sugar before serving.

name: Rwandan Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish rubbed with garlic and lemon, reflecting Rwanda's freshwater fishing tradition around Lake Kivu.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and lemon juice, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.

name: Rwandan Sweet Potato Fritters
description: Simple fried sweet potato fritters, a common Rwandan snack, real technique squeezing excess moisture from the grated sweet potato first.
steps_detailed: Squeeze the grated sweet potato well to remove excess moisture, then mix with the flour.
Fry spoonfuls, turning, 3-4 minutes, until golden and cooked through.
